questions.question: In a franchise, which party grants the rights to use the brand and business methods?
questions.explanation: The franchisor owns the brand and system and grants the rights; the franchisee invests in and operates the local business.

questions.question: A franchisor licenses its brand together with operating procedures, staff training, marketing support, service standards and reporting systems. Which arrangement is this?
questions.explanation: Business-format franchising licenses a broader system. Product and trade-name franchising licenses specified products under the franchisor's name, usually with less control over the whole operation.

questions.question: Which statement about the initial franchise fee is correct?
options: It is the only cost of entering a franchise
It is one part of the investment; premises, equipment, stock, staff and working capital may also be needed
It is refunded after the first year
questions.explanation: The fee is only one part of the investment, so a franchisee must estimate the complete commitment.

questions.question: A new outlet opens close enough to an existing franchisee to take its customers. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Encroachment is a new outlet or channel close enough to hurt an existing franchisee.

questions.question: What is churning?
options: Terminating and reselling an operation to collect more fees
Opening two outlets in one area
questions.explanation: Churning is terminating and reselling an operation in order to collect more fees. It is something to investigate, not something every franchise does.

questions.question: A franchise has monthly revenue of P100,000 and pays a 6% royalty. How much is the royalty?
The same franchise also pays a 1% advertising contribution. How much revenue remains after both payments?
questions.explanation: The royalty is P6,000 and the advertising contribution P1,000, together P7,000. P100,000 - P7,000 = P93,000. This is not profit, because stock, wages, rent and other expenses still have to be paid from it.

questions.question: Why can a revenue-based royalty be a burden on a franchisee?
options: It is due even when the outlet makes little profit or a loss
It is only paid in profitable years
It is paid by the customer
questions.explanation: Royalties based on revenue are due whether or not the outlet is profitable.

questions.question: What range of royalty do the class slides give as typical?
questions.explanation: The slides give 4% to 8% of gross revenue for royalties, and 1% to 3% for the advertising contribution.

questions.question: A franchise has monthly revenue of P100,000 and pays 6% royalty and 1% advertising. Stock costs P55,000, wages P20,000, rent P10,000 and utilities P3,000, with no other costs. What is left after everything is paid?
questions.explanation: After the fees P93,000 remains. Other costs are P55,000 + P20,000 + P10,000 + P3,000 = P88,000. P93,000 - P88,000 = P5,000.

questions.question: What is the first step in evaluating a franchise?
questions.explanation: The seven steps begin with an honest assessment of whether the franchise suits your abilities, capital and the independence you want.

questions.question: Why should a prospective franchisee speak to former franchisees as well as current ones?
options: Former franchisees always give the best advice
It is a legal requirement everywhere
They can explain why they left, and several sources are better than one favourable account
questions.explanation: Former franchisees can explain what went wrong or why they left. Use several sources, not one favourable account.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four reasons for buying an existing business?
questions.explanation: The four reasons are reducing uncertainties, ongoing operations and relationships, a favourable price and faster entry. None of them guarantees a profit.

questions.question: What is due diligence?
options: A fee paid to a broker
The systematic investigation of a business opportunity before committing to it
questions.explanation: Due diligence helps the buyer verify the seller's claims, identify obligations and decide whether the business is worth the price.

questions.question: An existing business is offered at a very low price. What should the buyer do?
options: Buy quickly before someone else does
Find out why the price is low, since it may reflect declining demand, damaged equipment or liabilities
questions.explanation: A favourable price is a benefit only if the reason for it is understood.

questions.question: A business shows rising profit because it sells on credit, but its customers are paying late. What is the main concern?
options: A profitable business can still run short of cash, especially during a change of ownership
questions.explanation: A credit sale adds to reported profit before the customer pays, so profit and cash flow can differ.

questions.question: A business has relevant assets with a fair value of P500,000 and liabilities of P180,000. What is its net asset value?
questions.explanation: P500,000 - P180,000 = P320,000. Which liabilities count depends on what is being acquired.

questions.question: Which valuation approach uses the prices paid for similar businesses?
questions.explanation: The market-comparable approach adjusts prices paid for similar businesses for size, location, profitability, assets and risk. Its limitation is that truly comparable deals can be hard to find.

questions.question: What is a main limitation of the asset-based approach?
options: It needs forecasts of cash flow
It may overlook earning capacity and goodwill
questions.explanation: Net asset value does not capture what the business can earn. The cash-flow-based approach does, but it is sensitive to forecasts.

questions.question: Which closing step holds the buyer's funds until the agreed conditions are met?
questions.explanation: Payment escrow holds the funds until conditions are met. The bill of sale transfers the assets, tax clearances confirm no tax obligations pass to the buyer, and lease assignment needs the landlord's consent.

questions.question: In the Two Men and a Truck case, what continuing payments did franchisees make?
options: A royalty of 6% of gross revenue plus 1% for advertising
questions.explanation: The case gives a royalty of 6% of gross revenue plus 1% for advertising, in addition to the initial fee. Treat the figures as historical case evidence, not current terms.
